name: Code Craft & Career
description: Naming, refactoring, code review, licensing, debugging discipline and the interview skills nobody teaches.

modules.name: Writing Code People Can Read
modules.description: Naming, structure, refactoring and error handling.

cards.prompt: What makes a good name?
cards.answer: It states intent, is pronounceable and searchable, and its length matches its scope — a loop index can be `i`, a module-level export cannot. Booleans read as predicates (`isReady`, `hasAccess`); functions are verbs; avoid encodings and unexplained abbreviations.
cards.explanation: Naming is the cheapest documentation there is: `getUserById` needs no comment, `process(data)` needs a paragraph. If a good name is hard to find, that is usually a sign the thing does more than one job.

cards.prompt: Which of these comments earns its place?
cards.answer: The second. The first restates the code and will rot; the second records *why*, which the code cannot express and no future reader could reconstruct.
cards.explanation: Comment the why, not the what: constraints, rejected alternatives, links to tickets and specifications, and warnings about non-obvious consequences. A comment explaining confusing code is often a refactoring you decided not to do.

resources.title: Stack Overflow Blog — Best practices for writing code comments

cards.prompt: What is refactoring, strictly, and what makes it safe?
cards.answer: Changing the internal structure of code without changing its observable behaviour. It is safe when tests cover that behaviour and each step is small enough to verify — otherwise it is a rewrite wearing a disguise.
cards.explanation: Never mix refactoring with behaviour change in one commit: a reviewer cannot see the real change inside a reformat, and a bisect cannot separate them. Common moves: extract function, rename, replace conditional with polymorphism, introduce parameter object.

cards.prompt: What are the rules of good error handling?
cards.answer: Fail fast and loudly; handle errors where you have enough context to act; never swallow an exception silently; preserve the original cause when wrapping; distinguish expected failures (invalid input) from bugs (null dereference); and include enough context to diagnose without a debugger.
cards.explanation: The worst pattern is `catch { /* ignore */ }` — it converts a loud failure into silent corruption discovered days later. Errors are part of your API: model expected failures in the type system where the language allows it.

cards.prompt: When should you optimise?
cards.answer: After measuring. Profile to find where the time actually goes, optimise that, and measure again. Before that, write the clearest correct code — except for algorithmic choices and data layout, which are expensive to change later.
cards.explanation: Knuth's line is usually truncated: the full quote allows that the critical 3% deserves attention. Intuition about hotspots is famously bad — the bottleneck is routinely an accidental O(n²), an N+1 query, or a serialisation nobody thought about.

cards.prompt: What is a systematic debugging method?
cards.answer: Reproduce it reliably, then form a hypothesis, then design an observation that would disprove it, then test. Bisect the space — in the code, in history, in the data — rather than reading everything. Change one thing at a time.
cards.explanation: The failure mode is changing things hopefully until the symptom moves, which produces fixes nobody understands and regressions later. If you cannot reproduce it, the first task is reproduction, not repair. Rubber-duck explanation solves a startling share of bugs before any tool is opened.

modules.name: Working & Interviewing
modules.description: Review, licensing, and the parts of the job that are not code.

cards.prompt: How do you give a good code review?
cards.answer: Review promptly. Separate must-fix from suggestion from nitpick, and say which is which. Ask questions instead of issuing verdicts. Comment on the code, never the author. Approve when it is better than what is there, not when it is perfect.
cards.explanation: Blocking on personal style preferences is the fastest way to make review adversarial — automate formatting so it never comes up. Praise good solutions explicitly; review that only ever finds fault trains people to write defensively rather than well.

resources.title: Google — How to do a code review

cards.prompt: Permissive vs copyleft licences
cards.answer: Permissive (MIT, Apache-2.0, BSD) lets you use the code in proprietary software with attribution. Copyleft (GPL, AGPL) requires derivative works you distribute to be released under the same licence.

left.title: MIT / Apache-2.0
points: Apache-2.0 adds an explicit patent grant

right.title: GPL / AGPL
points: Derivatives must be GPL when distributed
AGPL extends this to network use (SaaS)
LGPL relaxes it for dynamic linking

cards.explanation: AGPL is the one to check before adopting a dependency in a hosted product — 'we never distribute binaries' is not an exemption. 'No licence' means all rights reserved: unlicensed code on GitHub is not free to use.

cards.prompt: How should you approach a coding interview question?
cards.answer: Restate the problem and confirm constraints. Give a brute-force approach and its complexity out loud. Improve it, explaining the insight. Only then write code. Walk through an example, then discuss edge cases and tests.
cards.explanation: Silent coding is the most common failure — the interviewer is assessing your reasoning, which they cannot see. Saying 'this is O(n²), I think a hash map makes it O(n)' scores even if you never finish. Ask clarifying questions; ambiguity is usually deliberate.

cards.prompt: What is the STAR method, and what makes a strong behavioural answer?
cards.answer: Situation, Task, Action, Result. A strong answer is specific, uses 'I' rather than 'we' for your own contribution, quantifies the outcome, and includes what you learned — especially when the story is about a failure.
cards.explanation: Prepare six or seven real stories covering conflict, failure, leading without authority, a hard technical decision, and a time you changed your mind. They will cover most questions asked. Rehearsed generic answers are transparent; concrete detail is what convinces.

cards.prompt: How do you keep learning effectively as a working engineer?
cards.answer: Learn depth-first from primary sources when you need something, and breadth-first through fundamentals that do not expire — data structures, networking, operating systems, databases. Build things. Read code written by people better than you. Space your revision instead of cramming.
cards.explanation: Frameworks turn over every few years; the layer beneath them barely changes, and it is what makes new frameworks easy to learn. Spaced repetition works because the testing effect — retrieving an answer — builds far stronger memories than re-reading it.

resources.title: Teach Yourself Programming in Ten Years (Norvig)

modules.name: Clean Code in Practice
modules.description: Code smells, guard clauses, function design, abstraction levels, KISS and YAGNI, static analysis and the boy-scout rule.

cards.prompt: Name common code smells and the refactoring each suggests.
cards.answer: Long method → extract function. Large class → extract class. Long parameter list → introduce a parameter object. Feature envy (a method using another object's data more than its own) → move method. Primitive obsession → value objects. Shotgun surgery (one change touches many files) → consolidate. Duplicated code → extract and share.
cards.explanation: A smell is a hint, not a verdict: it tells you where to look. Refactor smells when you are about to change that code anyway, with tests in place, one small step at a time.

cards.prompt: How would you make this easier to read?
cards.answer: Replace the nesting with guard clauses that handle invalid cases and return early: `if not user: return None`, `if not user.active: return None`, `if not order.items: return None` — leaving the main logic unindented at the end.
cards.explanation: Deep nesting forces readers to keep every condition in their head at once. Early returns put the exceptional cases first and let the happy path read straight down. The same idea appears as `let ... else` in Rust and `guard` in Swift.

resources.title: Refactoring.Guru — Replace nested conditional with guard clauses

cards.prompt: What makes a function well designed?
cards.answer: It does one thing at one level of abstraction, has a name that says what it does, takes few parameters (group related ones into an object), avoids boolean flag arguments that switch behaviour, has no hidden side effects, and returns results rather than mutating its inputs where practical.
cards.explanation: A boolean flag (`render(doc, true)`) is a sign of two functions sharing a body — split them or pass a named option. Separating commands (which change state) from queries (which return data) makes code easier to reason about and test.

cards.prompt: What is the single level of abstraction principle?
cards.answer: Statements within a function should sit at the same level of abstraction. A function that orchestrates high-level steps (`validate(order); charge(order); notify(customer)`) should not also contain low-level byte manipulation or string formatting in the middle.
cards.explanation: Mixed levels force the reader to switch between "what" and "how" line by line. Extracting the low-level parts into well-named helpers turns the top-level function into a readable summary — the code becomes its own outline.

cards.prompt: A teammate adds a plugin system, a configuration DSL and an abstract base class "so we can support other payment providers later". There is one provider and no plans for another. What principle applies?
cards.answer: YAGNI — "you aren't gonna need it" — and KISS — "keep it simple". Build for the requirement you have; speculative generality has real costs today (code to read, test and maintain) for a benefit that may never come, and it is often designed around the wrong future.
cards.explanation: Simple code is easier to change when the second provider really arrives, and at that point you will know what actually varies. YAGNI is not an excuse for poor structure — keep code clean and well separated so later extension is cheap.

cards.prompt: What should automated formatting, linting and type checking take off a team's plate?
cards.answer: Formatters (Prettier, Black/ruff format, gofmt, rustfmt) end style debates; linters (ESLint/oxlint, ruff, clippy, golangci-lint) catch bug patterns and unsafe constructs; type checkers (tsc, mypy/pyright) catch type errors before runtime. All run in the editor for instant feedback and in CI as a gate.
cards.explanation: Anything a machine can check should never appear in code review. Adopt rules gradually on legacy code (baseline existing violations) and treat new warnings as errors, so the codebase only gets better.

cards.prompt: What is the boy-scout rule, and how do you apply it without derailing a change?
cards.answer: "Leave the code better than you found it": when you touch code, make small improvements nearby — rename an unclear variable, extract a confusing block, add a missing test. Continuous small clean-ups stop decay without big rewrites.
cards.explanation: Keep the improvements small and put them in a separate commit (or PR) from the behaviour change, so reviewers can see each clearly. Large refactors deserve their own planned change, not a detour inside a bug fix.

resources.title: 97 Things Every Programmer Should Know — The Boy Scout Rule

modules.name: Working with Others
modules.description: Design documents and RFCs, pair and mob programming, legacy seams, and docstrings versus comments.

cards.prompt: What belongs in a design document or RFC, and when is one worth writing?
cards.answer: Context and the problem, goals and explicit non-goals, the proposed design, alternatives considered and why they were rejected, risks and open questions, and a rollout and testing plan. Write one when a change is hard to reverse, spans teams, or has several reasonable approaches.
cards.explanation: The document is a thinking tool: writing down alternatives exposes weak reasoning before code exists, and review catches problems while they are cheap. Keep it short, and record the final decision as an ADR so the "why" survives.

cards.prompt: Pair programming vs mob (ensemble) programming
cards.answer: In pairing, two developers work on one task at one machine — one drives, one navigates — swapping often. In mobbing, the whole team works on one thing together, rotating the driver every few minutes.

left.title: Pair programming
points: Good for tricky code and onboarding

cards.explanation: Both trade raw parallelism for fewer defects, shared knowledge and no review queue. Use them for hard problems, onboarding and risky changes rather than all day. Remote tools make both practical; rotate roles frequently so nobody just watches.

cards.prompt: What is a seam in legacy code?
cards.answer: A place where you can change the code's behaviour without editing it in that place — typically by injecting a dependency, overriding a method in a test subclass, or swapping an implementation through configuration. Seams let you put untestable code under test.
cards.explanation: Legacy code often constructs its dependencies internally (`new Database()` inside a method). Introducing a seam — passing the database in, with the old construction as a default — is often the first safe refactoring, enabling characterisation tests.

resources.title: Michael Feathers — Working Effectively with Legacy Code

cards.prompt: API documentation (docstrings) vs inline comments
cards.answer: Docstrings document a function's contract for callers — what it does, parameters, return value, errors raised, examples — and feed IDE tooltips and generated docs. Inline comments explain non-obvious implementation choices for maintainers.

left.title: Docstring / doc comment
points: Shown in IDEs and generated docs

right.title: Inline comment
points: Rarely needed if code is clear

cards.explanation: Public APIs deserve docstrings; private helpers with good names often do not. Executable examples in docs (doctests, Rust doc tests) keep documentation from drifting out of date.
